title: Putting up holiday lights in Vero Beach? A plain safety check for cords, outlets and older wiring
seoTitle: Vero Beach Holiday Lights: Electrical Safety Tips
description: Decorating your Vero Beach home? How to check cords and outlets, the warning signs of an overloaded circuit, and ladder and palm tree tips before lights go up.
dek: The yard is drying out and the decoration bins are coming down from the attic. Before you wrap the palms and plug in the reindeer, here is a short, sourced checklist that keeps the season merry and the breakers quiet.
facebook: Getting the holiday lights out early this year? Before you wrap the palm trees, take five minutes for this check: which cords belong outside, the warning signs your outlets are overloaded, and the ladder rule most of us forget.
keywords: Christmas lights electrical safety older home
outdoor extension cord GFCI holiday lights
Christmas lights on palm trees safety

body.text: It has been a long, wet week in Vero Beach. Preliminary National Weather Service reports show 13 to 16 inches of rain across Indian River County from last week's storm. Now the sun is back, Thanksgiving is less than three weeks out, and a lot of us are eyeing the box of lights in the garage.

Holiday lights are one of the few times a year we ask our house's wiring to do a lot more than usual, often through cords that spent eleven months in a hot attic. This guide walks through what the Electrical Safety Foundation International (ESFI) recommends, in plain words, with a few notes for Florida yards.

body.title: The short version
body.text: Use only cords and decorations rated for outdoor use outside. Plug outdoor lights into GFCI-protected outlets. Check every string for damage before it goes up. Keep cords out of standing water. Turn everything off when you leave or go to bed. And if your breakers trip often or an outlet feels warm, stop and call a licensed electrician.
Start on the garage floor, not the ladder

Before anything goes on the house, plug each light string in on the ground and look it over. ESFI says to check lights, decorations and cords for damage before using them. Look for cracked or cut insulation, broken sockets, loose bulbs and plugs that are bent or scorched. If a string is damaged, it is cheaper to replace it than to gamble with it.

Next, sort indoor from outdoor. ESFI says to use only extension cords and electrical decorations rated for outdoor use outside. The rating is printed on the package or on a tag on the cord. Indoor-only lights on a porch railing in Florida dew are asking for trouble.
Also check that each extension cord can handle the amperage of everything plugged into it. ESFI lists that as its own rule. A thin indoor cord feeding three inflatables and a spotlight can overheat.

A GFCI (ground-fault circuit interrupter) is the outlet with the little "test" and "reset" buttons. It shuts off power fast if electricity starts going where it should not, like through water or a person. ESFI says outdoor decorations should be plugged into GFCI-protected circuits. If your outdoor outlets do not have that protection, ESFI says you can buy a portable GFCI at an electrical supply store and use it without special skills.

After last week's flooding, some low yards and swales are still soggy. ESFI says to keep cords and light strings out of standing water. Route cords along higher ground, and keep the connection points off the grass.
Signs your house is working too hard

ESFI says overloaded electrical circuits are a major cause of home fires. A power strip adds places to plug in, but ESFI points out it does not add any power to the outlet behind it. Watch for these warning signs that ESFI lists:

items: Lights that flicker, blink or dim
Breakers that trip or fuses that blow often
Wall plates that feel warm or look discolored
Outlets that crackle, sizzle or buzz
A burning smell near an outlet or switch
A mild shock or tingle from an appliance, outlet or switch

body.text: If you see any of these, unplug the decorations on that circuit and have a qualified electrician take a look. ESFI also says that if you rely heavily on extension cords, that is a sign your home has too few outlets, and an electrician can inspect the house and add more. If you live in an older home and find an extension cord in every room, that tip is for you.

Inside, ESFI recommends plugging major appliances straight into the wall, and only one heat-producing appliance into an outlet at a time. That matters in December, when the space heater, the coffee maker and the tree can end up sharing a wall.
In Vero, a lot of lights go on palm trees and rooflines. ESFI's ladder and tree tips:

items: Use a wooden or fiberglass ladder, not metal, because metal conducts electricity.
Check the ladder for loose or missing hardware before you climb.
Pick a ladder tall enough to reach at least three feet past the roof edge.
Keep yourself and your equipment at least 10 feet from power lines. Look up before you raise a ladder or a pole next to a palm.
Fasten lights to the tree, house or another sturdy support so wind does not tear them down, but do not staple or pinch through the cord's insulation.
Give spotlights airflow, weather protection and room away from anything that can burn.
Pull out the bins and test every light string on the ground. Toss anything with damaged cords or sockets.
Separate indoor-only items from outdoor-rated ones. Only outdoor-rated cords and decorations go outside.
Find your outdoor outlets and press "test" and "reset" on any GFCI. If there is no GFCI protection, pick up a portable GFCI.
Plan your cord routes on high, dry ground, away from doors and windows where cords can get pinched.
Spread the load across more than one circuit. If a breaker trips, do not just reset it and keep adding lights.
Set a timer, or make it a habit: ESFI says to turn off indoor and outdoor decorations before you leave home or go to sleep. Unplug a string before you change a bulb or fuse.
If you notice warm outlets, buzzing, burning smells or frequent tripping, call a licensed electrician before the lights go back on.

body.text: None of this takes long. A half hour on the garage floor now can save a lot of trouble on a December night.

faq.q: Can I use indoor Christmas lights outside in Florida?
faq.a: No. The Electrical Safety Foundation International says to use only lights, decorations and extension cords that are rated for outdoor use outside. Check the package or the cord tag for the rating.

faq.q: Do outdoor holiday lights need a GFCI outlet?
faq.a: ESFI says outdoor decorations should be plugged into GFCI-protected circuits. If you do not have one outside, a portable GFCI from an electrical supply store can be used without special skills.

faq.q: How do I know if my outlet is overloaded?
faq.a: ESFI lists warning signs: flickering or dimming lights, breakers that trip often, warm or discolored wall plates, buzzing or crackling outlets, a burning smell, or a mild shock from a switch or appliance. Unplug and call a qualified electrician if you notice any of them.

faq.q: How far should a ladder be from power lines when hanging lights?
faq.a: ESFI says to keep yourself and your equipment at least 10 feet from power lines, and to use a wooden or fiberglass ladder rather than a metal one.

faq.q: Should I leave Christmas lights on overnight?
faq.a: ESFI recommends turning off all indoor and outdoor decorations before you leave home or go to sleep. A timer makes that easy.
